“Quite apart from the possibility that philosophical ideas may develop independently and in parallel in different countries with similar social conditions—a possibility that this hypothesis clearly ignores altogether—there is another point to consider.
“For a foreign, ‘borrowed’ idea to take root in new soil, that soil must already be prepared to receive it.

“So even if we accept that Greek influence helped shape the ideas of Nyaya–Vaisheshika, we still have to study the social conditions in India—conditions which, in their general features, may have resembled those of Greece. Only those conditions could have made the acceptance and further development of these ideas possible.

“There is another point as well. Those who support the idea of complete and wholesale borrowing ignore the fact that the Nyaya Sutra and the Vaisheshika Sutra, although they remind us in some respects of Democritus, Plato, and Aristotle, contain a great deal more than we find in those thinkers.

“Moreover, those three ancient Greek philosophers did not, in the final analysis, represent the same philosophy that appears in Nyaya–Vaisheshika. Nor did they hold the same atomic theories, the same related ideas, the same judgments and conclusions, or the same philosophical categories. These things are not simply the same as they were in Greek philosophy. Here, in Nyaya–Vaisheshika, they appear as parts of a new Indian philosophy.”
We therefore need to look at Indian atomism in its own right, rather than treating it in exactly the same way as Greek atomism.
Two questions need to be answered.
What were the main ideas in the atomic theories of Nyaya–Vaisheshika?
And how did this school understand essence?
Indian thinkers spoke of nine kinds of essence.
The first four, however, had a special place in their philosophy: earth, water, fire, and air.
Each of these four essences could be understood in two forms: an eternal form and a non-eternal form.
Chattopadhyaya explains the distinction as follows:
“By the eternal form of these essences they meant their atoms. By the non-eternal form they meant the combinations formed from those atoms.

“According to the Nyaya–Vaisheshika theory, atoms are not all alike in quality. Atoms of earth differ qualitatively from atoms of water and from the atoms of the other essences. The same is true of the atoms of water, fire, and air.”
Here we can see one difference between the atomism of Democritus and that of Nyaya–Vaisheshika.
But there was also another intellectual current in India, known as the Jaina tradition, which was interested in atomism.
Its interest was less intense than that of Nyaya–Vaisheshika, but the Jaina current had already taken shape several centuries before that school.
It also differed from Nyaya–Vaisheshika in an important respect: it accepted the idea that atoms were qualitatively alike.
So the disagreements over atomism did not exist only between Indian and Greek philosophy. They also existed among the different Indian atomic schools themselves.
In any case, the followers of Nyaya–Vaisheshika tried to prove that atoms differed qualitatively.
They argued in roughly the following way:
Even the tiny particles that we can see only in a beam of sunlight entering a room through a small opening are not ultimate particles. They too are made up of smaller parts.
But this process of division cannot continue forever. There must be some point at which it ends.

Their reasoning was that if division were truly infinite, size itself would ultimately disappear as a meaningful difference. We could then say, for example, that an atom and a mountain were equal, since there would be no real difference in size between them.
From the claim that the chain of smaller parts must eventually come to an end, and that atoms can no longer be divided beyond that point, they concluded that atoms are not eternal.

Following this logic, the question of the creation of the world could be raised only together with the question of its disappearance, because if we accept disappearance, we must also accept coming into existence.
On this question of coming into existence and passing away, they reasoned as follows:
If atoms are infinite, there is no need to ask when they began.
But all ordinary things are temporary.
This means that they have both a beginning and an end.
If we now compare the atomism of Nyaya–Vaisheshika with that of the ancient Greek school, what do we find?
Let us look again at Chattopadhyaya, who states the issue very directly:
“Our view of the atomic theory of Nyaya–Vaisheshika must be connected with our view of its relationship to the corresponding theory in ancient Greece.

“In the history of ancient Greek philosophy, Democritus proposed the atomic hypothesis as a rational way of solving the problems of his age, especially problems that had already been raised by thinkers such as Parmenides and Heraclitus.”
“Parmenides, to some extent, has a parallel in the idealism of the Upanishads, since he recognized one reality: a single, unchanging being.
“Heraclitus, on the other hand, was in some respects like our early Buddhists. For him, the only reality was change, or becoming.”
We can understand Chattopadhyaya’s point in the following way.
In Greece, atomism first appeared as an attempt to solve the problems raised by two opposing views.
On one side stood Parmenides, who spoke of true being and denied change.
On the other stood Heraclitus, who recognized nothing except change.
The Upanishads insisted on a single, unchanging being.
Buddha, by contrast, recognized only change.
Buddha used the image of a candle flame to describe this constant change, just as Heraclitus used the image of flowing river water.
If this is what Chattopadhyaya means, then the comparison leads to a further conclusion.

Just as the ancient Greek atomists tried to find a way of reconciling the view of Parmenides with that of Heraclitus, the Indian atomists tried to find a way of reconciling the Upanishadic view with the early Buddhist view.
“It is not difficult to see the strong similarity with the situation faced by the followers of Nyaya–Vaisheshika.
“On one side stood the teaching of the Upanishads, with its eternal and unchanging Brahman. On the other stood the Buddhist doctrine of a continuous stream—the stream of change.
“The followers of Nyaya–Vaisheshika found a way out of this contradiction through atomic theory.
“They argued that eternal, unchanging atoms could explain being, while the different ways in which those atoms combine, separate, and recombine could explain becoming.
“But the Nyaya–Vaisheshika system lacked many important elements of Democritus’s theory, especially one of its central elements: the motion of atoms.”
Chattopadhyaya then comments on this last point:
“Nyaya atomism developed, to some extent, in the opposite direction.
“Kanada, one of the founders of the Nyaya school, did not even mention God. He was most likely an atheist.
“Later philosophers who followed this method, however, were not merely believers in God. They found themselves in the front ranks of those who offered proofs for his existence.
“Why did our atomism meet this particular fate?
“Perhaps we can trace it back to the level of technology through which Nyaya thinkers tried to understand the problem of creation.

“As we noted earlier, they understood the creation of a thing as the result of bringing together the parts from which it is made. Their standard example was the production of a pot by joining its parts together. This method of production is called kabala and is still used in our country in pottery.

“Because the followers of Nyaya tried to understand the production of everything through this same model, they also explained the creation of things made from atoms as basically a process of combining atoms.
“But if this is a process of bringing things together, then there must be someone who brings them together.
“In this way, a place was opened within the Nyaya system for ‘God,’ who was called upon to fill this gap in the atomic hypothesis.”

There is no doubt that Chattopadhyaya’s way of framing the question deserves attention. But if we look at the issue more broadly, on the level of society as a whole, it is useful to remember what Marx said on this subject:

“Historical periods differ from one another not in what they produce, but in how they produce it. So there is nothing unreasonable about connecting the way ideas are produced with the way material goods are produced.”

Of course, it would be wrong to derive the way ideas are produced—and especially their content—mechanically from the way material goods are produced. This does not mean rejecting Chattopadhyaya’s conclusion. But we do need to add the influence of earlier ideas and intellectual traditions, above all religious traditions, which have always had, and still have, an especially powerful influence on Indian culture.

We should also remember that mystical theories did not develop in a vacuum. They too were shaped by a whole range of political and intellectual traditions. Even Epicurus, despite his reputation for atheism, still spoke about the gods. In Indian philosophy, religious traditions were much stronger. Alongside changes in technology, these traditions were among the factors that helped change the form taken by atomism in the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika school.
In explaining how the followers of this school understood divine intervention in the movement of atoms, the Indian philosopher Shastri writes:

“The atomic theory of the Nyāya system included the assumption that the will of almighty God awakens in the atoms the necessary effects of the actions and conduct of the souls, or jīvas, that reside in bodies. It also awakens in them different kinds of activity connected with the qualities inherent in the atoms. Under the influence of this activity, atoms join together in pairs, groups of three, groups of four, and so on. Creation (sṛṣṭi) takes place in this way. If the jīvas no longer require creation in this form, the almighty will of God produces other kinds of activity in the atoms. These cause them to split apart, destroying the forces that hold two atoms together in a pair, and the atomic combinations then dissolve, beginning with the pair.”

We have gone into this much detail about Greek and Indian atomic theories for a deliberate reason. These are the two main ancient sources of atomism, and we wanted to present them clearly enough, both historically and scientifically, to make a serious comparison possible between them and the atomic theories found in the Arab-Islamic intellectual tradition.
Only then can we make a sound judgment about the older sources from which Arab atomists may have borrowed, or drawn inspiration, when developing theories of their own.
We might even say that this detailed account of Greek and Indian atomism helps fill a gap in modern Arab knowledge of the subject.
After this extended overview of atomic theories in ancient philosophy, one further comparison may help complete the picture: the difference between ancient and modern ideas about the atom.
The first thing that stands out is one basic difference between the ancient view and the modern one. It may even be the decisive difference.

Ancient thinkers—Democritus above all—believed that division must eventually reach a final point, beyond which the atom could no longer be divided. Modern science, by contrast, has shown through experiment that the atom can continue to be divided without such a final limit.

There is another difference as well. Ancient theories did not solve the problem of what holds the parts of an atom together, or what holds atoms together when they form different combinations. Different answers were proposed, but none reached the heart of the problem. On this point, they all remained trapped within a rather simple way of thinking.

Modern science, by contrast, was able to solve the problem through the development of experimental methods and technology. It showed that when atoms meet, they bind together through chemical affinities that arise between them.

Yet despite the many deep differences between ancient and modern thought in this field, we still have to recognize that modern chemistry and physics rest, at a fundamental level, on Democritus’s theory and developed from the assumptions with which he began.

In the nineteenth century, Cournot wrote in his Study of the Sequence of Fundamental Ideas in the Sciences and in History (p. 245) that no idea inherited from antiquity had reached anything like the importance of Democritus’s idea of the atom.

Galileo almost certainly knew the teachings of Democritus. Pierre Gassendi, who helped bring atomic theory into modern science, began from his study of Epicurus, the great continuator of Democritus. Even Descartes, who rejected atomic theory, was so deeply influenced by Democritus in his mechanical explanation of nature that, in a letter to Mersenne dated 30 August 1640, he had to answer the accusation that he had done little more than patch up the worn-out clothes of Democritus.
We should also mention what Kedrov wrote about atomism in the Great Soviet Encyclopedia:

“The view that atoms never change, that they are incapable of development or qualitative transformation, that the relations between them are purely external and mechanical, and that they possess no motion except mechanical motion—this is the view characteristic of the metaphysical and mechanical conception of atoms, that is, of old atomism.

“The dialectical conception of atoms, confirmed by modern science, is characterized instead by the view that atoms are capable of change, that they form a successive series of stages of development that grow qualitatively more complex, that they continually enter into both organic and inorganic combinations governed by definite patterns, and that they are in permanent and uninterrupted motion.”
E — The Atomic Question in Arab-Islamic Thought
We have now reached the point toward which this long discussion of the different ancient forms of atomism has been leading.

Our aim is to identify the source from which Arab-Islamic thought took the basic elements of atomism and then brought them into Islamic theological debate, reshaping them according to its own outlook and giving them a largely independent character.
There are two questions we need to examine.

The first is the source used by the earliest Arab-Islamic thinker to introduce the idea of the “indivisible part” into Islamic thought. As we have already seen, that thinker was Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf.
